meta.title: Who really said "They also serve who only stand and wait"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: it is line 14 of John Milton's sonnet, printed as Sonnet XVI in his Poems (1673). The title 'On His Blindness' was added by an editor in 1761.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'They also serve who only stand and wait'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Milton: line 14 of Sonnet XVI in his Poems (1673). But the famous title isn't his, and the speaker is Patience, not the poet.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1608–1674 · English poet; Secretary for Foreign Tongues to Cromwell’s Council of State
answer.sourceLine: It is line 14 — the closing line — of the sonnet beginning “When I consider how my light is spent,” printed as Sonnet XVI in Milton’s Poems, &c. upon several occasions (London, 1673). The 1673 text reads “They also serve who only stand and waite”; the only difference from the wording quoted today is the old spelling.

source.heading: The source: Sonnet XVI, Poems (1673)

docMeta.dd: Sonnet XVI — “When I consider how my light is spent”
Poems, &c. upon several occasions, London: printed for Tho. Dring, 1673
Most scholars date it June–October 1655; possibly as early as 1652
Line 14, the sonnet’s closing line, spoken by Patience

source.excerpt:
Doth God exact day-labour, light deny’d,
I fondly ask ; But patience to prevent
That murmur, soon replies, God doth not need
Either man’s work or his own gifts, who best
Bear his milde yoak, they serve him best, his State
Is Kingly. Thousands at his bidding speed
And post o’re Land and Ocean without rest:
They also serve who only stand and waite.
trail: The line is line 14 of Milton’s sonnet beginning “When I consider how my light is spent,” printed as Sonnet XVI — Wikisource’s transcription of the 1673 text ↗ ends it exactly: “They also serve who only stand and waite.”

That transcription checks out against the book itself. The 1673 first edition scanned at the Internet Archive ↗ — London, printed for Tho. Dring, from the Princeton Theological Seminary copy — carries the sonnet under the heading “XVI.”
Dartmouth’s John Milton Reading Room ↗ prints the same 1673 wording, and Wikiquote ↗ files the line among its sourced Milton quotations, not among the misattributions.

Wikipedia’s article on the sonnet ↗ records the publication history: first printed in Milton’s 1673 Poems, numbered 19 in his own Trinity Manuscript but 16 in the printed book, with the title “On His Blindness” assigned later by Thomas Newton.
source.excerptNote: Reproduced with the 1673 first edition’s own spelling and punctuation — “waite” for “wait,” “milde yoak” for “mild yoke.” Modern editions silently modernise all of it.

author.name: John Milton
author.heading: About John Milton
author.metaLine: 1608–1674 · English poet, polemicist and civil servant
author.bio: John Milton was an English poet, polemicist and civil servant who served as Secretary for Foreign Tongues to the Council of State from 1649 to 1660, composing the Commonwealth’s official Latin correspondence. He was totally blind by 1652 and dictated the work of his later years, including Paradise Lost, published in 1667. The sonnet that ends with this line belongs to the same decade in which he lost his sight, and was first printed in the 1673 collection of his Poems.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is solid — this is Milton, in a book printed in his lifetime. What travels badly is everything around the line: the title, the speaker, the spelling and the sonnet number.

items.why: The sonnet is almost always quoted under this title, but Milton never gave it one. Wikipedia ↗ notes there is no evidence Milton used it; it was assigned by the editor Thomas Newton in his 1761 edition. In 1673 the poem ran with no title at all — just the number XVI.

Quoted alone, the line reads as a blind poet consoling himself. Inside the sonnet it is Patience, personified, who cuts off his complaint and speaks the closing lines — a point Interesting Literature ↗ makes explicitly.

items.who: “They Also Serve, Who Stay and Wait” · “We Also Serve”
items.why: Both are adaptations, not Milton’s words. Wikipedia ↗ lists the Navy Wives Clubs of America motto “They Also Serve, Who Stay and Wait” and the Dickin Medal’s “We also serve”; the medal itself ↗ is inscribed “For Gallantry” and “We Also Serve.”

Citations disagree because Milton and his printer did. Wikipedia ↗ records that he numbered it 19 in his autograph Trinity Manuscript while the 1673 book numbered it 16, and both numbers are used in modern scholarship.

misattribution.truthLine: Milton wrote it, and it was printed in a book published in his lifetime: the closing line of the sonnet numbered XVI in Poems, &c. upon several occasions (1673) ↗, where it is spelled “stand and waite.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Milton was totally blind by 1652, in the middle of his working life as Secretary for Foreign Tongues to the Council of State — the man who drafted the English republic’s Latin correspondence. The sonnet is his argument with himself about what that loss meant. It opens close to panic, with the biblical parable of the talents turned against him: “that one Talent which is death to hide, / Lodg’d with me useless.”

The famous last line is the reply, not the complaint — and it is not Milton speaking. Patience interrupts to say that God needs neither man’s work nor his own gifts; thousands rush at his bidding across land and ocean, and those who simply stand ready serve just as fully. Milton wrote it in the 1650s; it did not reach print until the 1673 collection of his Poems.
context.detailsSummary: Why the line keeps getting borrowed
detailsBody: Stripped of the sonnet, the line becomes a general-purpose consolation for anyone sidelined — the reservist, the carer, the family at home. That is why it survives as institutional motto more than as quotation: the Dickin Medal ↗ for animals in wartime service is inscribed “We Also Serve,” and the Navy Wives Clubs of America adopted “They Also Serve, Who Stay and Wait.”
Read in place it is narrower and stranger: a theological claim that God is not short-handed, addressed to a man who has just lost the ability to do the work he believed he existed to do.
context.pull: “God doth not need / Either man’s work or his own gifts”

sourcesVerified.claim: OCR of the scanned 1673 first edition shows the sonnet under the heading "XVI.", beginning "When I consider how my light is spent" and ending "They also serve who only stand and waite."
This Internet Archive item is the 1673 edition of Milton's Poems, &c. upon several occasions, London, printed for Tho. Dring, from the Princeton Theological Seminary Library copy.
Wikisource transcribes the sonnet from the 1673 Poems under the heading "XVI." with the closing line "They also serve who only stand and waite."
Dartmouth College's John Milton Reading Room prints the sonnet with the final line "They also serve who only stand and waite."

The sonnet was first published in Milton's 1673 Poems; he numbered it 19 in the Trinity Manuscript but the printed book numbered it 16; the title "On His Blindness" was assigned by Thomas Newton in his 1761 edition with no evidence Milton used it; it was most likely composed between June and October 1655, possibly as early as 1652; the Dickin Medal motto "We also serve" and the Navy Wives Clubs of America motto "They Also Serve, Who Stay and Wait" are variants of the final line.

Wikiquote lists "They also serve who only stand and wait" in its sourced section for John Milton, credited to "When I Consider How My Light is Spent"; its Misattributed section contains a different quotation entirely (Sarah Ban Breathnach).
The Dickin Medal bears the words "For Gallantry" and "We Also Serve" within a laurel wreath.

John Milton was born 9 December 1608 and died 8 November 1674; he was an English poet, polemicist and civil servant; he served as Secretary for Foreign Tongues to the Council of State from March 1649 to May 1660; he had become totally blind by 1652; Paradise Lost was published in 1667.
The closing line is spoken within the sonnet by Patience personified, not by Milton in his own voice.
This line appears on the list of quotations commonly misattributed to Shakespeare.
